problemSolved: A strict inspect-then-build sequence delays feedback until everything is extracted, and lets small extraction gaps accumulate silently across a whole page before anyone notices.
mechanism: Explicitly frames the process as NOT two-phase: 'a foreman walking the job site' who inspects one section, writes its spec, hands it to a builder, and keeps walking — extraction and construction happen in parallel, section by section, rather than as two monolithic passes.
whyItWorks: Keeps each unit of work small and independently checkable (one section's spec, one section's build) instead of one giant extraction document feeding one giant build. Failures stay local to a section rather than compounding across the whole page.
requiredContext: a host that supports dispatching parallel sub-agents/worktrees mid-task
outputImpact: Structural, not stylistic — affects how work is sequenced, not what the output looks like.
failureModes: Requires a runtime capable of true parallel sub-agent dispatch (git worktrees); degrades to a slower serial version without it, and the skill gives no fallback instruction for that case.
conflicts: None internal. External: SiteSmith's redesign task edits an existing codebase in place — it does not need a fresh-clone target to build into, so the 'builder writes a new file in a worktree' half of this mechanism does not transfer as-is.
testMethod: Asserted only — no measurement of whether interleaving actually reduces gaps versus a strict two-phase run.
sitesmithForm: Keep the underlying discipline (extract one section, verify it fully, only then move on) for SiteSmith's audit-before-redesign step, but drop the parallel-worktree-builder half — the audit step measures the existing site, it does not need to dispatch construction agents against it.

problemSolved: Without stated defaults, 'clone this site' is ambiguous about fidelity level and scope, forcing either a clarifying question every time or silent scope creep/shrinkage.
mechanism: States explicit defaults up front — fidelity level (pixel-perfect), in-scope items (visual layout, structure, interactions, responsive, mock data), out-of-scope items (real backend, auth, real-time, SEO, accessibility audit) — and a single override clause: user instructions beat the defaults.
whyItWorks: Converts an implicit assumption into an explicit, falsifiable statement the user can override in one sentence, without requiring a question-and-answer round trip before work starts.
requiredContext: none — self-contained
outputImpact: Prevents scope disputes after the fact by naming the default scope before work starts.
failureModes: A user who doesn't read the defaults may be surprised that accessibility/SEO were silently excluded — the override clause only helps if the user knows to invoke it.
sitesmithForm: Give SiteSmith's audit/redesign entry point the same shape: state the default fidelity bar and explicit in/out-of-scope list for the audit pass in one short block, overridable by the user's own words.

problemSolved: A skill that hard-codes one specific browser-automation tool breaks entirely in any environment that has a different one, or none.
mechanism: Checks for any of several browser MCP tools (Chrome MCP, Playwright MCP, Browserbase MCP, Puppeteer MCP), prefers Chrome MCP if multiple exist, and explicitly asks the user how to connect one if none is detected — stating the skill cannot function without it.
whyItWorks: Detect-and-degrade-gracefully beats hard-coding a single dependency; the explicit 'ask the user' fallback avoids a silent failure or a confusing error deep in the workflow.
requiredContext: knowledge of which browser-MCP tool names to check for
outputImpact: Portability across host environments; no effect on output quality once a tool is found.
failureModes: The list of tool names is a fixed enumeration and will go stale as new browser-automation MCPs appear — no mechanism updates it.
sitesmithForm: Apply the same detect-preferred-tool-then-ask-if-none pattern to SiteSmith's own audit step, since it likewise has a hard browser-automation dependency for extracting live-site truth.

problemSolved: A builder handed an incomplete spec fills gaps by guessing (a color, a padding value), and the guess is invisible in the output — it just looks slightly wrong.
mechanism: States the principle directly: if a builder has to guess anything, extraction has already failed; take the extra minute to extract one more property rather than ship an incomplete brief.
whyItWorks: Names the actual failure condition ('the builder guessed') rather than a vague 'be thorough' instruction, giving the extracting agent a concrete self-test: would the receiving agent need to guess anything reading this spec?
requiredContext: the component spec being written must be checked against this test before dispatch
outputImpact: Directly reduces silent, hard-to-detect fidelity drift caused by unstated assumptions.
failureModes: Asserted only — nothing checks whether a builder actually did guess; the test is self-applied by the same agent writing the spec, with no external verification (see TESTING.md).
sitesmithForm: Reuse verbatim as a self-check question at the end of SiteSmith's audit-extraction step: 'would someone rebuilding this section from only what I wrote down have to guess anything?'

problemSolved: A single agent given an entire complex section ('build the features section') approximates spacing and font sizes rather than nailing them, because the scope is too large to hold every exact value in mind.
mechanism: A mechanical, numeric threshold: if a builder prompt would exceed roughly 150 lines of spec content, the section must be split into one agent per sub-component plus one wrapper agent. Stated explicitly as 'a mechanical check — don't override it with but it's all related.'
whyItWorks: Removes judgment from the split decision, which is exactly where judgment tends to be optimistic ('it's fine, it's all related'). A hard numeric line is falsifiable in a way 'use good judgment about complexity' is not.
requiredContext: a draft or estimate of the spec file's line count before dispatch
outputImpact: High for output precision — the source's own claim is that per-component focus is what makes an agent 'nail it every time' versus 'approximate.'
failureModes: A 150-line threshold is an arbitrary constant tuned to this pipeline's spec-file verbosity; porting it to a differently-shaped spec format without re-deriving the right threshold could make the rule either meaningless (never triggers) or overly aggressive (splits everything).
testMethod: Asserted only — no measurement comparing split vs. unsplit builder output quality.
sitesmithForm: Keep the underlying principle (a numeric ceiling on scope-per-unit-of-work forces splitting, overriding 'but it's related') for any SiteSmith step that hands work to a sub-agent, but re-derive the actual line-count number against SiteSmith's own spec/prompt format rather than reusing 150 verbatim.

problemSolved: A section that visually reads as 'one image' is frequently multiple stacked layers (background gradient, foreground mockup PNG, overlay icon); extracting only the most obvious image makes the rebuild look empty even when the background is correct.
mechanism: Explicit instruction to inspect every container's full DOM tree and enumerate ALL `` elements and background-images within it, including absolutely-positioned overlays, repeated as a named failure mode ('Don't miss overlay/layered images... a background watercolor + foreground UI mockup = 2 images').
whyItWorks: Names a specific, easy-to-miss failure pattern (single visual impression, multiple DOM layers) concretely enough that an agent can check for it directly, rather than relying on a general 'extract all images' instruction that a single top-level `` scan would already satisfy while still missing the overlay.
requiredContext: DOM access to the container being inspected, including computed `position`/`z-index`
outputImpact: Medium-high for visual fidelity of any section using layered/composited imagery — a common pattern in modern marketing hero sections.
failureModes: Only covers image layering; does not generalize the same vigilance to layered CSS effects (gradients, blend modes, filters) applied without any ``, which could be equally invisible if only checking for image tags.
sitesmithForm: Carry the specific check ('walk the container DOM tree, count every img and positioned background-image, not just the first one you notice') into SiteSmith's asset-extraction step verbatim as a named anti-pattern to check for.

problemSolved: Extracting only static computed CSS makes a rebuild look right in a screenshot but 'feel dead' the moment a real user scrolls, hovers, or clicks — because a website is a living thing, not a screenshot.
mechanism: Requires every element's appearance (exact `getComputedStyle()` values) AND behavior (exact trigger, before/after states, transition mechanism) to be captured, backed by an illustrative, non-exhaustive list of 13 named behavior categories (scroll-triggered header changes, viewport-entry animations, scroll-snap, parallax, animated hover, modal/dropdown transitions, scroll-driven progress, auto-cycling carousels, theme transitions, tab-cycling, scroll-driven tab switching via IntersectionObserver, smooth-scroll libraries).
whyItWorks: Static-CSS-only extraction is the obvious failure mode for any cloning task; naming 13 concrete behavior categories gives the extracting agent a checklist to scan for rather than relying on noticing behaviors incidentally while looking at something else.
requiredContext: the ability to trigger each behavior category live (scroll, click, hover, wait) via browser automation
outputImpact: High — this is explicitly framed as the difference between a clone that looks right in a screenshot and one that feels right in use.
failureModes: The list is explicitly 'illustrative, not exhaustive' (SKILL.md:67) — an agent that treats it as a closed checklist rather than a prompt to keep looking will miss behaviors outside the 13 named categories.
testMethod: Asserted only — no instrumented behavior-diffing tool ships with the repo; extraction is manual scripted `getComputedStyle()` calls before/after a triggered state change.
sitesmithForm: Reuse the appearance-plus-behavior split and the 13-category behavior checklist (re-expressed in SiteSmith's own words) as the audit step's definition of what 'fully extracted' means for an interactive section, explicitly flagging it as a starting list to extend, not a closed set.

problemSolved: Named as 'the single most expensive mistake in cloning': building a click-based UI when the original is actually scroll-driven (or vice versa) requires a full rewrite, not a CSS tweak.
mechanism: A strict investigation order: scroll through the section slowly first and watch for unprompted change; only if nothing changes on scroll do you then test click/hover. The determined model (click-driven / scroll-driven / hover-driven / time-driven / static) must be written explicitly into the component spec before any builder prompt is written.
whyItWorks: Ordering the investigation (scroll-before-click) directly counters an availability bias: click-testing is the more habitual first move for testing UI, but scroll-driven behavior (IntersectionObserver-triggered tab switching, sticky-panel scrollytelling) is invisible unless scrolled first and easy to misdiagnose as click-driven if clicked first.
requiredContext: the section must be scrolled through slowly before any click testing begins
outputImpact: High — explicitly the highest-cost mistake class the source names, because misdiagnosis here costs a full rebuild rather than a style fix.
failureModes: Relies on the agent actually following the stated order under time pressure — nothing external gates or checks that scroll-testing happened before click-testing.
testMethod: Asserted only, but named as the single most expensive class of mistake based on the source's own retrospective ('lessons from previous failed clones,' SKILL.md:448).
sitesmithForm: Make 'scroll before you click, and write down which interaction model you found, before writing any spec for an interactive section' a mandatory ordered step in SiteSmith's audit pass — this is a cheap, concrete rule with a named, expensive failure mode if skipped.

problemSolved: Extracting only whatever is visible on page load misses every other tab's content, every post-scroll header style, every hover state — components with multiple states get documented as if they only had one.
mechanism: Requires clicking every tab/button and capturing its content and computed styles separately, and for scroll-dependent elements, explicitly capturing state at scroll position 0, then again past the trigger threshold, then diffing the two captures to identify exactly which CSS properties changed — 'the diff between A and B IS the behavior specification.'
whyItWorks: Turns 'document the hover/scroll behavior' from a narrative description into a mechanical two-snapshot-and-diff procedure, which produces exact before/after property values rather than an approximate description of what changed.
requiredContext: ability to trigger each state (click tab, scroll past threshold, hover) and re-run the extraction script per state
outputImpact: High for any stateful component — this is what makes multi-state components (tab bars, scroll-morphing headers) reproducible rather than approximated.
failureModes: Cost scales with number of states — a component with many tabs or many scroll thresholds means many extraction passes; no guidance on when to stop for components with a very large or continuous state space.
testMethod: Asserted only, but the diffing procedure itself is a measurement (two real `getComputedStyle()` snapshots compared), which is stronger than the source's own Phase-5 fidelity check (see FAILURE-MODES.md).
sitesmithForm: Adopt the two-snapshot-diff procedure as SiteSmith's standard method for documenting any stateful element found during audit, rather than a prose description of 'what changes.'

problemSolved: Hand-measuring individual CSS properties one at a time is slow and invites the exact estimation errors ('it looks like text-lg') the source explicitly warns against (SKILL.md:454).
mechanism: A concrete, reusable JavaScript snippet that walks a component's DOM to depth 4, calls `getComputedStyle()` against a fixed list of ~40 named properties per element, and filters out properties at their default/no-op value (`none`, `normal`, `auto`, `0px`, transparent) so the output is only meaningfully-set values, plus per-node tag/classes/direct-text/image metadata.
whyItWorks: A single script call replaces dozens of manual property inspections with one structured JSON dump, and the default-value filter keeps the output signal-dense (real numbers, not noise) rather than dumping every computed property regardless of whether it matters.
requiredContext: a CSS selector for the target container
browser MCP execution capability
outputImpact: High — this is the concrete tool underneath every 'exact computed style' claim elsewhere in the skill; without it those claims would be unenforceable.
failureModes: Depth-4 traversal and a 20-child cap (SKILL.md:269,278) will silently truncate very deep or very wide component trees, producing an incomplete spec with no warning that truncation occurred.

The fixed property list is a snapshot of what mattered to this repo's author; a target site using a CSS feature outside the list (e.g. `clip-path`, `mask`, container queries) would be silently missed.
testMethod: This is itself a measurement tool — real `getComputedStyle()` values, not an estimate — making it one of the few genuinely measured (not asserted) mechanisms in this source.
sitesmithForm: Port this extraction script's structure (depth-limited DOM walk, fixed-but-extensible property list, default-value filtering) as SiteSmith's standard truth-extraction tool for the audit-before-redesign step, extending the property list to cover the CSS features it omits.

problemSolved: A builder told 'see DESIGN_TOKENS.md for colors' either doesn't read it, misreads it, or the reference drifts out of sync with the actual extracted values — and a builder given only whatever fits in a short prompt guesses to fill gaps.
mechanism: Every component gets a dedicated spec file, written from a fixed template (overview, DOM structure, computed styles per element, states/behaviors with trigger/before/after/transition, per-state content, assets, verbatim text, responsive breakpoints), and the full contents of that file — not a pointer to it — are pasted inline into the builder agent's prompt. The rule is stated twice as a named anti-pattern: 'Don't reference docs from builder prompts' and 'Don't dispatch builders without a spec file.'
whyItWorks: The spec file forces exhaustive extraction as a side effect of having to fill every template section, and inlining it removes any chance the builder skips a referenced file — the builder literally cannot proceed without the values already being in front of it.
requiredContext: nothing external — this is precisely the point: zero external file reads required by the builder
outputImpact: High — described as the mechanism that prevents 'incomplete instructions based on whatever you can remember from a browser MCP session.'
failureModes: Spec files persist as artifacts (SKILL.md:112) but nothing enforces that the inlined copy pasted into a builder's prompt stays byte-identical to the file on disk if either is edited later — drift between artifact and prompt is possible with no detection.
testMethod: Asserted only for the 'no guessing' claim, but the fixed template format is itself a checkable structure (every section either filled or explicitly marked N/A, SKILL.md:375).
sitesmithForm: Adopt both halves — a persistent, template-shaped spec artifact per unit of work, and always inlining its full contents rather than referencing it — for any SiteSmith step that hands extracted truth to a build/fix step.

problemSolved: Manually finding and downloading every image/video/background-image/font/favicon on a page one at a time is slow and easy to under-count.
mechanism: A single DOM-query script enumerates every `` (with parent-layering metadata), `
whyItWorks: One enumeration pass produces a complete inventory before any downloading starts, so the download step has a fixed, known list rather than discovering assets incrementally and risking missed ones; batching (4 at a time) balances speed against overwhelming the source server or the local network stack.
requiredContext: browser MCP execution for the enumeration script
a Node/JS runtime to write and run the download script
outputImpact: Medium-high — directly determines completeness of the visual asset set the rebuild will have available.
failureModes: The enumeration script is described as something to run and then 'write a download script' from — it is not itself a checked-in, reusable tool (confirmed: no `download-assets.mjs` exists in the repo, only `scripts/.gitkeep`), so its quality is re-derived by the agent every single run rather than hardened once.
testMethod: The enumeration script is a real measurement (actual DOM query); the download step's completeness is only as good as that one enumeration pass, with no post-download verification that every URL found was actually fetched successfully.
sitesmithForm: Reuse the single-enumeration-pass-then-batch-download pattern for SiteSmith's asset audit, but harden it as an actual checked-in script rather than an agent-authored-from-scratch script each run, since the pattern itself doesn't change between runs.

problemSolved: Building every section serially, one after another in the same working tree, is slow and blocks extraction of later sections on the completion of earlier builds.
mechanism: Every builder agent works in its own git worktree branch; the foreman does not wait for a builder to finish before moving on to extract the next section; as worktrees complete, the foreman merges them into main, using its own cross-agent context to resolve conflicts, reverifying `npm run build` after every merge.
whyItWorks: Git worktrees give each builder an isolated working directory without needing a full separate clone, enabling genuine parallel file edits without collision, while the foreman's single vantage point across all dispatched work is what makes intelligent conflict resolution possible at merge time.
requiredContext: a host agent runtime capable of dispatching and tracking multiple concurrent sub-agents
local git worktree support
outputImpact: Throughput/speed, not output quality per se — a section built this way is not inherently more faithful than one built serially, only built sooner.
failureModes: Heavy orchestration machinery: requires a runtime that supports concurrent sub-agent dispatch and git worktree management, which not every host or task provides.
Merge-conflict resolution quality depends entirely on the foreman's judgment, with no described gate beyond 'resolve intelligently' and a build check.
conflicts: Directly conflicts with SiteSmith's redesign task shape: an audit-before-redesign step measures the existing site's truth, it does not need to spin up N parallel construction agents against a fresh scaffold. This mechanism belongs to a hypothetical 'rebuild elsewhere' product, not an in-place audit.
testMethod: Asserted only — no measurement of actual time saved or conflict-resolution accuracy.
sitesmithForm: Do not adopt for the audit step. If a future SiteSmith mode does need to reconstruct a site from scratch in a new codebase, the worktree-per-unit-of-work pattern is worth revisiting then — but it adds orchestration complexity without measurable value for an audit-and-report task.

problemSolved: Nominally, confirming the finished rebuild actually matches the source.
mechanism: Take screenshots of the original and the clone at the same viewport widths (1440px, then 390px), compare them section by section by looking, and for each discrepancy found, check whether the spec was wrong (re-extract, fix spec, fix component) or the spec was right but the builder deviated (fix component). Also re-walk all interactive behaviors manually (scroll, click every button/tab, hover every element).
whyItWorks: It doesn't measure anything — it is a narrative instruction to look and compare, identical in kind to the self-critique step in `frontend-design` (same-model, self-graded, no external check), just applied to fidelity instead of originality.
requiredContext: screenshots of both original and clone at matching viewports
outputImpact: Whatever the agent's own visual judgment catches, and nothing it doesn't — this is the entire fidelity gate for the whole pipeline.
failureModes: No pixel-diff tool, no similarity score, no pass/fail threshold anywhere in the 61-file repo — despite every earlier phase being unusually rigorous about measured, computed-style extraction, the final fidelity check reverts entirely to eyeballing.
The rigor of extraction (Phases 1-3) creates a false impression that fidelity itself is measured; it is not — only the inputs to the build are measured, the output-vs-source match is asserted.
conflicts: This is the single clearest instance in this source of the 'REDESIGN task audits before touching, fidelity should be measured not asserted' principle being violated — the extraction is measured, but the thing the whole pipeline exists to guarantee (the clone matches the source) is checked by the same unaided narrative process that a much smaller, cheaper skill would use.
testMethod: Asserted only — confirmed by direct inspection: no script in this repo computes an image diff, DOM diff, or CSS diff between source and output.
sitesmithForm: Do not adopt this specific mechanism as SiteSmith's fidelity gate. If SiteSmith's redesign task needs a before/after fidelity check, it should use an actual measured comparison (structural CSS/DOM diff, or a real perceptual-diff tool) rather than narrated screenshot comparison — this is exactly the kind of claim SiteSmith's own `scripts/verify.mjs` philosophy (measure, don't assert) already rejects elsewhere.

problemSolved: Without an explicit stopping point, extraction can feel 'done enough' and dispatch happens on an incomplete spec.
mechanism: A 9-item checklist (spec file written and complete, every CSS value from getComputedStyle not estimated, interaction model documented, all states captured, hover before/after recorded, all images including overlays identified, responsive documented for at least desktop+mobile, text verbatim, prompt under ~150 lines) that must be fully satisfied before any builder is dispatched — 'if you can't, go back and extract more.'
whyItWorks: A checklist gate applied at a single well-defined moment (immediately pre-dispatch) is cheap to apply and catches the same gaps the rest of the skill describes in prose, restated as yes/no items rather than narrative guidance — easier to self-audit against in the moment.
requiredContext: the draft spec file to check against
outputImpact: Consolidates the skill's scattered completeness requirements into one checkable moment rather than trusting they were all followed along the way.
failureModes: Self-applied and self-graded — nothing external confirms the checklist was actually run item-by-item rather than skimmed and assumed satisfied.
testMethod: Asserted only, but each item is individually checkable in principle (e.g. 'every value from getComputedStyle' can be spot-checked against the spec text).
sitesmithForm: Reuse the pattern of consolidating a pipeline's scattered completeness rules into one explicit pre-handoff checklist, re-derived for whatever SiteSmith's audit step actually hands off (a redesign brief, not a builder-agent spec).

problemSolved: Generic 'be careful' guidance doesn't transfer lessons from actual past mistakes; without naming them, the same mistake recurs.
mechanism: A 12-item 'What NOT to Do' list, explicitly framed as 'lessons from previous failed clones — each one cost hours of rework' — e.g. building click-based tabs for a scroll-driven original, extracting only the default tab state, missing layered images, mockup-building content that's actually video, approximating Tailwind classes instead of extracting exact values, referencing external docs from builder prompts.
whyItWorks: Each item names a specific, concrete failure observed in practice (not a hypothetical), which is more actionable than an abstract principle — this mirrors the same technique frontend-design uses for its named-cliché list (naming the enemy concretely rather than saying 'avoid clichés').
requiredContext: none — self-contained, but implicitly a living document that should grow as new failure classes are observed
outputImpact: Medium — reinforces (via repetition and specificity) the same rules stated earlier in the Guiding Principles section, functioning as a compressed final-pass reminder.
failureModes: Framed as drawn from 'previous failed clones' but there is no mechanism in the repo that actually captures new failures and appends them — it is committed prose, frozen at whatever failures were known when last edited, with the same staleness risk as any hand-maintained list.
sitesmithForm: Keep a similarly concrete, specifically-worded 'named failure' list for SiteSmith's audit step, and treat it explicitly as a living list to extend when new failure classes are actually observed, not a document copied once and left static.

problemSolved: Supporting 13 different AI coding agents (README.md:58-72) with their own native instruction-file formats would otherwise mean hand-maintaining 13 near-duplicate files that drift out of sync.
mechanism: Two single-source-of-truth files (`AGENTS.md` for project instructions, `.claude/skills/clone-website/SKILL.md` for the slash command) plus two regeneration scripts. `sync-agent-rules.sh` resolves a Claude-Code-style `@file` import syntax (`AGENTS.md:65`) and writes 4 generated instruction files for agents that don't read `AGENTS.md` natively. `sync-skills.mjs` reads the SKILL.md frontmatter+body and writes 9 platform-specific command files in each platform's own format (TOML for Gemini, JSON for Amazon Q, YAML-frontmatter Markdown for the rest), logging an exact count on completion (`sync-skills.mjs:112`).
whyItWorks: Treating platform-specific config as a build artifact (generated, headed with 'do not edit directly,' regenerated by a script) rather than as hand-maintained parallel copies is a standard single-source-of-truth pattern that eliminates drift by construction.
requiredContext: contributors must remember to run the sync scripts after editing either source file — nothing enforces this automatically (no pre-commit hook, no CI check verifying generated files are current)
contextCost: n/a — this is a repo-maintenance mechanism, not something loaded into a task-execution context
outputImpact: None on the quality of any individual clone — this only affects how many coding-agent platforms can invoke the skill at all.
failureModes: Nothing prevents the generated files from silently drifting if a contributor edits `AGENTS.md` or `SKILL.md` and forgets to re-run the corresponding script; the generated copies would look current (they have real content) while actually being stale.

The CRLF-handling fix in CHANGELOG.md ('0.3.1 — sync-agent-rules.sh failing to resolve @file imports on Windows due to CRLF line endings') shows this exact staleness/breakage class has already happened once in this repo's own history.
conflicts: Not applicable to SiteSmith as currently scoped: SiteSmith is being unified into ONE skill for one host (this project's own Claude Code / Codex / Grok trio, per the project's CLAUDE.md), not distributed as a template repo targeting 13 external agent platforms. Building this sync machinery would be complexity with no current consumer.
testMethod: Not tested by any script — the sync scripts themselves have no test suite; the CHANGELOG entry above is evidence a real breakage occurred and was caught by a human, not by automated verification.
sitesmithForm: Not applicable to the current SiteSmith rebuild goal (one unified skill, not a 13-platform template distribution). If SiteSmith is ever repackaged for multi-platform distribution, the single-source-plus-regeneration-script pattern is sound and worth revisiting then, with a CI check added that the earlier repo's own history shows is missing.
